prohibited_recommendations: Do not give verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers or IV amiodarone for pre-excited atrial fibrillation
Do not discharge without an electrophysiology study and ablation plan
Do not attribute the palpitations to work stress and the syncope to a vasovagal reaction
required_recommendations: Recognise syncope with ventricular pre-excitation and documented orthodromic AVRT as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, a high-risk cause of syncope
Admit with continuous ECG monitoring and a defibrillator available until the accessory pathway is treated
Refer for an electrophysiology study and catheter ablation of the accessory pathway during this admission or urgently (ESC 2019 SVT Class I)
For recurrent orthodromic AVRT: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine with a defibrillator available; synchronised cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable
If pre-excited atrial fibrillation occurs: synchronised cardioversion if unstable, IV procainamide or ibutilide if stable; no AV-nodal blocking drugs or IV amiodarone (ESC 2019 SVT Class III)
Advise no driving and no competitive sport until the pathway has been ablated (ESC 2018)

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case with classic WPW triad on ECG (short PR, delta waves, wide QRS) in a young patient presenting with syncope. The ECG findings clearly point to the diagnosis with minimal confounders.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Carlos Delgado is a 40-year-old right-handed man who presents to the emergency department after an episode of sudden loss of consciousness that occurred approximately 90 minutes ago while at work. According to three coworkers who witnessed the event, Mr. Delgado was standing at his desk reviewing inventory reports when he suddenly collapsed to the ground without any preceding warning symptoms. The witnesses reported that his eyes rolled back, he became pale, and he was unresponsive for approximately 15 to 20 seconds. There were no tonic-clonic movements, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence during the episode. He regained consciousness spontaneously and was described as immediately lucid, able to answer questions about what he had been doing moments before the event, and oriented to his surroundings within seconds of awakening. He denied any preceding lightheadedness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, or visual changes before losing consciousness. He reports no aura, no unusual smells or tastes, and no focal weakness or numbness after the event. He has no prior history of syncope, seizures, or episodes of loss of consciousness. He denies recent illness, fever, changes in medications, excessive caffeine intake, or use of any new supplements. He had a normal breakfast this morning and was well-hydrated. He reports that over the past three months, he has occasionally noticed brief episodes where his heart felt like it was racing for a few seconds while at rest, but these were fleeting and he dismissed them as being related to stress at work. He has never sought medical attention for these sensations. His coworkers called emergency medical services, and on arrival the paramedics documented a regular pulse at 74 beats per minute, blood pressure of 118/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 99 percent on room air. He remained fully alert and oriented during transport and denied any recurrence of symptoms.
